records.source: Google Engineering Practices Documentation (eng-practices)
records.population: Google engineering, all languages and projects, distilled from internal guidance
records.version_or_commit: master branch as published at google.github.io/eng-practices; repository archived read-only 2025-11-21
records.licence: CC BY 3.0 (documents); Apache-2.0 for any code
records.finding: Review approves on a health gradient, not a perfection bar: approve once the change definitely improves overall code health even when imperfect, refuse only what definitely worsens it, and separate design judgement (arguable on engineering grounds) from style (settled by the style guide, never by reviewer taste). The author-side guide makes small changes the mechanism that makes this affordable, because reviewers can find five minutes repeatedly but not thirty minutes once.
records.applicability_limits: Written for a very large monorepo with mandatory readability certification, ownership files and dedicated review tooling. A solo or two-person venture has no reviewer pool, so the health-gradient rule transfers but the ownership and readability machinery does not. The repository is archived, so it is a fixed historical artefact and will not track agentic review practice.
records.counter_evidence: FRAG-CODING-04 argues every stated goal of human review can be met by agents; the archive status is itself weak evidence that Google no longer treats this text as living guidance.
records.review: on-change-of:any successor to google/eng-practices or an un-archive of the repository

records.source: Sadowski, Soderberg, Church, Sipko, Bacchelli, Modern Code Review: A Case Study at Google
records.study_design: Exploratory mixed-method case study: interviews, survey and log analysis of Critique review data
records.population: Google engineers and their change-list review logs, circa 2017
records.licence: unknown (author-hosted preprint; IEEE/ACM proceedings copyright applies to the published version)
records.finding: At scale, review converges on small, single-reviewer, low-iteration changes: the majority of changes are small with one reviewer and no comments beyond the approval, around 70 per cent of changes are committed under 24 hours after being sent for review, and over 80 per cent involve at most one round of comment resolution. Review is sustained for education, norm-setting and gatekeeping as much as for defect finding.
records.applicability_limits: Single-company study inside a monorepo with bespoke tooling and a strong ownership culture; the latency and iteration figures are descriptive of that environment, not a target other teams have been shown to achieve. Pre-dates LLM authorship entirely, so nothing here speaks to reviewing machine-written diffs.
records.counter_evidence: FRAG-CODING-03 finds the defect-finding expectation is largely unmet in a different company; FRAG-CODING-04 disputes that human review remains the right instrument at all.

records.source: Bacchelli and Bird, Expectations, Outcomes, and Challenges of Modern Code Review
records.study_design: Multi-method: observations, interviews, survey of managers and developers, manual classification of review comments
records.population: Microsoft product teams using tool-based review
records.licence: unknown (publisher-hosted author copy; ICSE 2013 proceedings copyright applies)
records.finding: Expectation and outcome diverge: finding defects is the stated top motivation but reviews yield far fewer defect findings than expected and deliver most of their value as knowledge transfer, team awareness and alternative solutions. The binding constraint on review quality is the reviewer's understanding of the change and its context, which tooling mostly fails to supply.
records.applicability_limits: One large company, 2013 tooling, human-authored code. The understanding constraint is the transferable part; the specific comment-category proportions are not.
records.counter_evidence: If knowledge transfer is the real product, a solo operator with agent authors gets little from ceremonial review, which weakens the case for mandatory review in small ventures.

records.source: The End of Code Review: Coding Agents Supersede Human Inspection
records.study_design: Position and synthesis paper; no new empirical data, argues from published benchmark results
records.model: surveys frontier coding agents circa late 2025
records.licence: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive licence to distribute (author copyright retained)
records.finding: The argument that mandatory human review no longer pays is now stated explicitly in the literature: agents can serve defect detection, style enforcement and awareness at lower cost, humans spend a reported 10 to 15 per cent of hours reviewing, and feedback routinely takes over 24 hours. The paper's own concessions are the useful part: hallucinated approvals, non-trivial vulnerability injection rates, unsolved prompt injection, weak architectural judgement, and an accountability gap when an auto-approved change causes harm, so it lands on ensemble review with human oversight reserved for high-risk changes.
records.applicability_limits: Not peer-reviewed and not empirical; it is an argument, not a measurement. Benchmark resolution rates on curated issues do not license claims about review of arbitrary production diffs. Treat as a well-formed hypothesis and as a checklist of the risks any review-automation policy must answer.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0010 (METR RCT) shows measured slowdown where practitioners believed in speed-up, so agent-capability arguments that assume perceived gains are real should be discounted.
records.review: on-change-of:peer-reviewed publication or empirical replacement for this preprint

records.source: DORA capability page, Trunk-based development
records.study_design: Practitioner guidance summarising DORA survey analysis (2016 and 2017 State of DevOps data cited on the page)
records.population: DORA State of DevOps respondents, tens of thousands of professionals across years
records.licence: CC BY 4.0 (Google LLC, site-wide notice)
records.finding: Trunk-based development is defined operationally by four measurable conditions rather than by ideology: three or fewer active branches, branch lifetime of hours not days, at least one merge to trunk per developer per day, and no code-freeze periods. These are stated as required practice for continuous integration and are associated with higher delivery and operational performance.
records.applicability_limits: Survey-based association, self-reported, not a controlled experiment, and the causal direction is asserted rather than demonstrated. The four thresholds assume a multi-developer team; for a solo or agent-driven repo the meaningful residue is merge cadence and the ban on code freezes, not branch counts.
records.counter_evidence: The page itself concedes that trunk-based development is a substantial change requiring new skills and meets organisational resistance, so adoption cost is real.
records.review: on-change-of:new DORA report revising the trunk-based capability

records.source: DORA, State of AI-assisted Software Development 2025
records.study_design: Annual cross-sectional survey with modelling; self-reported measures
records.model: AI coding assistants generally, not a named model
records.version_or_commit: 2025 report as published on dora.dev, accessed 2026-08-03
records.licence: CC BY 4.0 (Google LLC, site-wide notice)
records.finding: AI amplifies the system it lands in rather than fixing it: adoption is near-universal (around 90 per cent), individual output rises sharply (reported figures around 21 per cent more tasks and far more pull requests merged), yet end-to-end delivery performance stays flat where the surrounding process is weak. Trust is low, with roughly a quarter reporting high trust and roughly a third little or none.
records.applicability_limits: Self-report, cross-sectional, no causal identification; the throughput figures measure activity, not delivered value. Aggregated across organisation sizes, so the flat-delivery result is about organisational bottlenecks that a one-person venture does not have in the same form.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0010 (METR RCT) measured a 19 per cent slowdown for experienced developers on their own repositories, directly contradicting self-reported throughput gains.
records.review: on-change-of:publication of the next annual DORA report

records.source: Conventional Commits specification
records.licence: CC BY 3.0
records.finding: A tiny grammar over commit subjects (type, optional scope, description, optional body and footers, with breaking change signalled by a bang or a BREAKING CHANGE footer) turns history into a machine-readable event stream: changelogs, version bumps and release triggers become derivations rather than manual work. The spec deliberately keeps only feat and fix mandatory and leaves further types to the team.
records.applicability_limits: Buys nothing unless something downstream actually consumes it (release automation, changelog generation, version selection); as decoration it is pure ceremony. Revert semantics are explicitly unspecified. The spec anticipates that not every contributor complies and suggests maintainer normalisation at merge, which matters when commit authors are agents.
records.counter_evidence: The spec's own FAQ concedes the risk that a fixed type vocabulary narrows the kinds of commit developers are willing to make.

records.source: Semantic Versioning specification
records.licence: CC BY 3.0
records.finding: Version numbers only carry meaning once a public API is declared precisely and comprehensively, in code or in documentation; MAJOR signals incompatible API change, MINOR backward-compatible addition, PATCH backward-compatible fix. Major version zero is an explicit escape hatch where anything may change at any time.
records.applicability_limits: The contract is only as good as the API declaration behind it; without one the numbers are decoration. Says nothing about how to decide compatibility for behavioural or performance changes, which is where most real breakage occurs. Ecosystems (npm ranges, Go modules) layer their own resolution rules on top.
records.counter_evidence: Date-based rolling versions with per-consumer pinning, as in EV-0061 (Stripe API versioning), solve the same coordination problem without semantic compatibility judgements.

records.source: Potvin and Levenberg, Why Google Stores Billions of Lines of Code in a Single Repository
records.study_design: Experience report with operational statistics; no comparison group
records.population: Google's Piper monorepo, reported at roughly 2 billion lines, 40,000 commits per working day, over 10,000 engineers
records.version_or_commit: Communications of the ACM vol 59 no 7 (2016), pages 78-87
records.licence: unknown (ACM copyright; the CACM web version is publicly readable)
records.finding: A monorepo buys one-version dependency management, atomic cross-project change and cheap large-scale refactoring, and it presupposes trunk-based development with essentially no long-lived branches. The report is candid that these benefits are bought with a bespoke tooling investment (Piper, CitC, build and analysis infrastructure) that most organisations cannot fund.
records.applicability_limits: The tooling cost is the whole story; quoting the benefits without the investment is the standard misreading. At venture scale the same benefits are available in a plain git monorepo precisely because the repo is small, so the paper argues for monorepo-by-default only in the small case and monorepo-with-heavy-tooling in the large case, with a painful middle.
records.counter_evidence: FRAG-CODING-10 catalogues the countervailing costs (tooling, build times, cross-team coupling, unclear ownership) reported by practitioners without Google-scale infrastructure.

records.source: Brito, Terra and Valente, Monorepos: A Multivocal Literature Review
records.study_design: Multivocal literature review, predominantly grey literature
records.population: Practitioner articles and talks on monorepo adoption
records.licence: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive licence (author copyright retained)
records.finding: The monorepo debate resolves into a named trade set rather than a winner: centralisation and standardisation give simplified dependencies, coordinated cross-project change and easy refactoring, and cost tooling investment, slower builds and weaker ownership boundaries. The decision is therefore about which costs you can pay, not which model is correct.
records.applicability_limits: Grey-literature synthesis, so it reports advocacy rather than measurement, and it is eight years old, predating the current generation of build and task tooling and predating agentic authorship entirely.
records.counter_evidence: FRAG-CODING-09 reports the monorepo benefits realised at extreme scale, which grey literature tends to over-generalise from.
records.review: on-change-of:a controlled or large-sample empirical comparison of monorepo and polyrepo outcomes

records.source: Yuan et al., Simple Testing Can Prevent Most Critical Failures (OSDI 14)
records.study_design: Retrospective manual analysis of 198 randomly sampled user-reported production failures
records.population: Cassandra, HBase, HDFS, Hadoop MapReduce, Redis
records.licence: unknown (USENIX open-access proceedings; USENIX and author copyright)
records.finding: Error handling is where catastrophe lives: 92 per cent of catastrophic failures studied came from incorrect handling of non-fatal errors that the software had already explicitly signalled, and about a third of those were trivial mistakes visible to plain code inspection with no system knowledge. Most failures reproduced on three nodes or fewer.
records.applicability_limits: Java-heavy distributed data systems circa 2014; the proportions are of that corpus. The transferable claim is the direction of attention, that the error path deserves more review and test effort than the happy path, not the exact percentage.
records.counter_evidence: None found that disputes the direction; later work generally reinforces error-path neglect.

records.source: The Go Blog, Working with Errors in Go 1.13
records.version_or_commit: published 2019-10-17, describing Go 1.13 errors.Is, errors.As and fmt.Errorf %w
records.licence: CC BY 4.0 for site content per the go.dev notice; code samples BSD-3-Clause
records.finding: Error identity is an interface decision, not a convenience: wrapping an error makes that error part of the caller-visible API, so wrap deliberately when callers should be able to react to the cause, and convert without wrapping when the cause is an implementation detail you refuse to commit to. Whatever you document as inspectable must always be returned that way, and inspection goes through chain-aware predicates rather than equality on a concrete type.
records.applicability_limits: Go-specific mechanics. The transferable rule is that the set of distinguishable failure modes is part of a module's contract and must be declared and versioned like any other part of it; languages with exceptions or Result types express the same rule differently.
records.counter_evidence: Ecosystems that treat all errors as opaque strings trade caller-side recovery for looser coupling; that is a real position, not an error, in throwaway or leaf code.
records.review: on-change-of:a Go proposal changing error inspection semantics

records.source: Feitelson, Mizrahi, Noy et al., How Developers Choose Names
records.study_design: Sequence of controlled naming experiments with blind analysis of chosen names
records.population: 334 subjects across the experiments, 47 naming instances
records.version_or_commit: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 2021; arXiv:2103.07487v1 preprint
records.licence: unknown (IEEE copyright on the published version; arXiv preprint under arXiv non-exclusive licence)
records.finding: Naming does not converge: the median probability that two developers pick the same name for the same thing was 6.9 per cent, yet a name once chosen is usually understood by most developers. Naming decomposes into choosing which concepts to encode, choosing words for each concept, and assembling them, which is what makes a review comment about a name actionable rather than a taste fight.
records.applicability_limits: Small controlled naming tasks, largely student and professional subjects on short scenarios, not whole-system naming under domain pressure. The asymmetry (low agreement, high comprehension) argues against enforcing name uniformity and for enforcing the concept-selection step.
records.counter_evidence: The high-comprehension result cuts against heavy naming review; if most names are understood anyway, review effort spent on renaming is largely wasted.

records.source: Silva, Tsantalis and Valente, Why We Refactor? Confessions of GitHub Contributors
records.study_design: Firehose monitoring of Java repositories for detected refactorings, followed by developer surveys about each specific refactoring
records.population: GitHub Java projects and their contributors; 44 distinct motivations across 12 refactoring types
records.licence: unknown (ACM copyright on the published version; arXiv preprint under arXiv non-exclusive licence)
records.finding: Refactoring in practice is overwhelmingly change-driven rather than smell-driven: developers refactor to make a specific pending change possible or to remove duplication encountered while working, and the catalogue of 44 motivations is dominated by these situational reasons rather than by detected code smells. This makes smell-detector-driven refactoring backlogs a poor model of how the work actually happens.
records.applicability_limits: Java, open source, 2016, and self-reported motivation with recall and social-desirability bias. Says nothing about whether the refactorings improved anything.
records.counter_evidence: FRAG-CODING-16 reports refactoring volume collapsing in AI-assisted codebases, which suggests the change-driven trigger is being bypassed rather than that the model is wrong.

records.source: Fucci et al., A Dissection of the Test-Driven Development Process: Does It Really Matter to Test-First or to Test-Last?
records.study_design: Regression modelling of four process characteristics (sequencing, granularity, uniformity, refactoring effort) against quality and productivity
records.version_or_commit: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 2017; arXiv:1611.05994 preprint
records.licence: unknown (IEEE copyright on the published version; arXiv preprint under arXiv non-exclusive licence)
records.finding: The active ingredient in test-driven development is not the sequencing. Quality and productivity were associated with granularity (small uniform work increments) and uniformity (a steady rhythm), not with whether the test came before or after the code. That reframes TDD as a work-decomposition discipline whose test-first ritual is optional scaffolding.
records.applicability_limits: Small sample, short greenfield tasks, human developers in a study setting; effect sizes are modest and the design is correlational within an experimental corpus. It does not license abandoning test-first where regression protection is the goal rather than developer productivity.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0003 (TDAD), EV-0004 (TDFlow), EV-0005 (TDDev) and EV-0007 (risk of coding before testing) all find sequencing matters substantially for agents, where tests supply the oracle the model lacks. The human and agent results are not in conflict once you see that the mechanism differs.

records.source: GitClear, The Maintainability Gap: 2026 AI Code Quality Research
records.study_design: Vendor observational study of git history metrics; non-random convenience sample of customer and public repositories; no control group; full method behind a lead-capture form
records.population: 623 million analysed changes, 2023 to 2026, including repositories owned by large technology firms
records.model: AI coding assistants in aggregate, not attributed per model
records.version_or_commit: January 2026 edition; charts stated to be updated quarterly
records.licence: unknown (no reuse licence stated; site terms of service apply)
records.finding: The measurable signature of AI-assisted codebases is structural rather than functional: refactoring line moves down about 70 per cent, cross-file function calls down about 35 per cent, within-commit copy and paste up about 41 per cent, block duplication up about 81 per cent, error-masking constructs up about 47 per cent, and two-week churn up about 15 per cent. Code gets written and does not get consolidated.
records.applicability_limits: Vendor-run, commercially motivated, sample not random and not disclosed in the public page, metrics are proxies chosen by the vendor and the causal attribution to AI is inferred from timing, not identified. Treat the direction as a hypothesis worth instrumenting locally, never the magnitudes as fact. Note in particular that duplication is not uniformly bad and that a single-owner venture may rationally tolerate more of it.
records.counter_evidence: FRAG-CODING-06 (DORA 2025) finds delivery outcomes flat rather than degraded, so the structural metrics have not been shown to translate into worse delivered outcomes.
records.review: on-change-of:next quarterly GitClear update or an independent replication

records.source: ApprovalTests.Python
records.version_or_commit: main branch as at 2026-08-03; supports Python 3.10 to 3.14
records.licence: Apache-2.0
records.finding: Characterisation testing is mechanised by inverting the assertion: capture current output as an approved artefact, diff every later run against it, and require a human to approve any change. This gets a behaviour net around code nobody understands in minutes, which is exactly the precondition for safe refactoring of inherited or agent-written code.
records.applicability_limits: Approved files lock in current behaviour including current bugs, so they are a refactoring safety net and never a specification. They rot into rubber-stamped diffs unless approval is a deliberate reviewed act. Poor fit for non-deterministic output unless scrubbers are applied.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0094 (write tests, not too many, mostly integration) warns against test volume that does not buy confidence; a large approved-file corpus is precisely that risk if approvals become reflexive.
records.review: on-change-of:a maintenance lapse in the approvals organisation repositories

records.source: Pearce, Ahmad, Tan, Dolan-Gavitt and Karri, Asleep at the Keyboard? Assessing the Security of GitHub Copilot's Code Contributions
records.study_design: Systematic prompt-completion experiment across diversity of weakness, prompt and domain, with static analysis and manual verification
records.version_or_commit: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2022; arXiv:2108.09293
records.licence: unknown (IEEE copyright on the published version; arXiv preprint under arXiv non-exclusive licence)
records.finding: Generated code is not security-neutral by default: roughly 40 per cent of generated programs in CWE-relevant scenarios contained a vulnerability, and the rate varied with the weakness class, the prompt and the domain. Prompt context, not model goodwill, is what moves the number.
records.applicability_limits: A 2021 model on deliberately security-loaded scenarios; the headline rate should not be applied to current models or to ordinary code. What survives is the structural claim, that a security gate must sit downstream of generation because generation quality varies with prompt and domain in ways the author cannot see.
records.counter_evidence: Later evaluations of newer models report lower rates; the finding is about the necessity of a gate, not the size of the number.
records.review: on-change-of:a current-model replication of the CWE scenario battery

records.source: Winters, Manshreck and Wright (eds), Software Engineering at Google
records.population: Google engineering practice as narrated by its practitioners
records.version_or_commit: first edition, March 2020, O'Reilly; free digital edition on abseil.io
records.licence: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (digital edition); no derivatives permitted, so extract principles only and never adapt the text
records.finding: Software engineering is programming integrated over time, so every construction rule should be justified by what it costs to keep the code alive rather than by what it costs to write. The corollaries used in practice are that code is read far more often than written, that expensive review is bought down by keeping changes small and reviewers few, and that any behaviour you want preserved must be defended by an automated test rather than by convention.
records.applicability_limits: No-derivatives licence constrains reuse of the text itself. Practices assume a monorepo, a build system that can run affected tests cheaply, and thousands of engineers; the time-integration principle transfers to a one-person venture but the review and ownership machinery does not.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0089 (harness design, Anthropic) warns that scaffolding encodes assumptions about model weakness and should be stripped as models improve; a long-lived practice corpus is exactly the kind of scaffolding that ossifies.

records.source: trunkbaseddevelopment.com
records.version_or_commit: site as served 2026-08-03; copyright notice reads 2017-2020
records.licence: unknown (no explicit reuse licence found; site copyright Paul Hammant with community contributions)
records.finding: Trunk-based development is specified as a ladder rather than a single practice: small teams commit straight to trunk, scaled teams use short-lived branches that exist only long enough for review and integration, and super-scaled teams add a merge or patch queue. Feature flags and branch by abstraction are the named mechanisms that make large changes compatible with continuous merging, and release branches are temporary and deleted.
records.applicability_limits: Practitioner site, opinion not measurement, and stale by copyright notice. It concedes the small-to-scaled boundary is debated, so the ladder positions are judgement calls. The flag and branch-by-abstraction mechanisms carry their own cost and their own cleanup discipline.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0026 (OpenFeature) shows the flag machinery this model depends on is itself a system needing lifecycle management, which small ventures often skip and then regret.
records.review: on-change-of:a refresh of the site or its replacement by a maintained equivalent
